title: svg-elements
content:
svg-elements

The svg-elements container groups SVG-related elements in the DITA technical content vocabulary. It provides the structural entry point for SVG markup used inside DITA content and is intended for safe inclusion of SVG content in technical documentation. Use this reference when authoring or validating SVG constructs in DITA 1.3 and later technical communication content.

Source: dita-lang technical content language reference.

title: <svg-container>
content:
<svg-container>

The <svg-container> element is a DITA container that can hold SVG content inside technical content topics. It is part of the svg-d domain and is used when authors need to embed SVG graphics as managed content instead of treating them as external binary images. This reference is relevant when explaining where SVG content is allowed, how it is wrapped, and how it differs from linking to standalone image files.

Source: dita-lang technical content language reference.

title: <svgref>
content:
<svgref>

The <svgref> element references SVG graphics in DITA technical content. It is used when an author needs to point to SVG-based graphic content through a dedicated DITA element rather than using generic prose or unrelated image markup. This page is part of the DITA technical content language reference and is useful for questions about valid SVG-related elements, SVG references, and conservative DITA authoring patterns around vector graphics.

Source: dita-lang technical content language reference.

title: syntaxdiagram-d
content:
syntaxdiagram-d

The syntaxdiagram-d container page describes the DITA syntax diagram domain used for command and language syntax notation in technical content. It groups the syntax-diagram-specific elements such as <groupseq>, <groupchoice>, <groupcomp>, <kwd>, <oper>, <delim>, <fragment>, <fragref>, and <repsep>. Use this reference when a question is about the syntax diagram domain as a whole rather than a single element.

Source: dita-lang technical content language reference.

title: <delim>
content:
<delim>

The <delim> element represents delimiter characters that appear in syntax notation. It belongs to the syntax diagram domain and is used to mark punctuation or separator characters as part of a command or language syntax expression.

Source: dita-lang technical content language reference.

title: <fragment>
content:
<fragment>

The <fragment> element contains a named fragment of syntax that can be defined once and then referenced elsewhere in a syntax diagram. It is part of the syntax diagram domain and helps authors model reusable subexpressions inside command or grammar notation.

Source: dita-lang technical content language reference.

title: <fragref>
content:
<fragref>

The <fragref> element references a syntax fragment defined elsewhere with <fragment>. It is used inside syntax diagrams when a reusable fragment needs to be included by reference instead of rewritten inline.

Source: dita-lang technical content language reference.

title: <groupchoice>
content:
<groupchoice>

The <groupchoice> element groups syntax items that represent a choice among alternatives. It is part of the syntax diagram domain and is useful when documenting commands or notations where one of several branches may be selected.

Source: dita-lang technical content language reference.

title: <groupcomp>
content:
<groupcomp>

The <groupcomp> element groups syntax items that form a composite or grouped expression within syntax notation. It is used in the syntax diagram domain when multiple items belong together as a single grouped unit.

Source: dita-lang technical content language reference.

title: <groupseq>
content:
<groupseq>

The <groupseq> element groups syntax items that occur in sequence. It is part of the syntax diagram domain and is used when the order of syntax tokens matters in the represented command or grammar.

Source: dita-lang technical content language reference.

title: <kwd>
content:
<kwd>

The <kwd> element marks a keyword or literal token in syntax notation. It is a core syntax diagram domain element used when documenting command names, literal options, or reserved words in a formal syntax pattern.

Source: dita-lang technical content language reference.

title: <oper>
content:
<oper>

The <oper> element marks an operator token in a syntax diagram. It belongs to the syntax diagram domain and is used when a syntax expression includes operators as meaningful parts of the notation.

Source: dita-lang technical content language reference.

title: <repsep>
content:
<repsep>

The <repsep> element marks the separator used between repeated syntax items. It is part of the syntax diagram domain and is useful when documenting lists or repeated arguments that use a visible separator in the syntax.

Source: dita-lang technical content language reference.

title: <synph>
content:
<synph>

The <synph> element represents a syntax phrase inside the DITA syntax diagram domain. It is used for inline syntax fragments and reusable syntax wording where phrase-level syntax markup is needed rather than a full block-level syntax diagram.

Source: dita-lang technical content language reference.

title: <synblk>
content:
<synblk>

The <synblk> element represents a block-level syntax container in the DITA syntax diagram domain. It is used when authors need block syntax markup rather than an inline syntax phrase, and it helps model larger syntax expressions in a conservative, structured way.

Source: dita-lang technical content language reference.

title: DITA-OT base parameters: args.draft
content:
DITA-OT base parameters: args.draft

The DITA Open Toolkit base parameter `args.draft` controls whether draft and cleanup content is included in generated output. For DITA-OT PDF / PDF2 builds where <draft-comment> must appear in the PDF, pass the parameter with a yes value. In the `dita` command-line syntax, parameters are supplied as command arguments in the form `--parameter=value`, so the practical argument is `--args.draft=yes`.

Use this source when the user asks which DITA-OT argument enables draft comments, draft output, or required-cleanup content in PDF output. In AEM Guides DITA-OT PDF output presets, this value belongs in the Additional DITA-OT Command Line Arguments field, not in a Native PDF template setting.

Source: DITA Open Toolkit development documentation.

Use `--args.draft=yes` with the `dita` command-line parameter syntax.

title: Arguments and options for the dita command
content:
Arguments and options for the dita command

The DITA Open Toolkit `dita` command requires the main file and output format for a normal transform, or a project file for multi-deliverable publishing. Core invocation forms: `dita --input=<file> --format=<transtype> [options]` and `dita --project=<file> [options]`. The short forms `-i file` and `-f name` correspond to the common parameters `args.input` and `transtype`. Input is usually a DITA map but may be a single topic; paths can be absolute, relative to `args.input.dir`, or relative to the current directory when `args.input.dir` is unset.

`--output=dir` / `-o dir` sets the output directory (`output.dir`); default is typically an `out` subdirectory. Pass arbitrary build parameters with GNU-style `--parameter=value` or Ant-style `-Dparameter=value`. Use `--propertyfile=file` for a `.properties` file; CLI values override the file. `--resource=file` / `-r file` supplies additional resource files (e.g. key map with a lone topic, or reltables map with a chapter map) and maps to `args.resources`.

`--filter=` accepts DITAVAL file paths; on Windows separate multiple paths with `;` inside quotes, on macOS/Linux use `:`, or pass `--filter=` multiple times (order matters; first wins on conflicts). `--temp=dir` / `-t dir` sets `dita.temp.dir`. For PDF, `--theme=file` applies a PDF theme configuration.

Subcommands (no transform): `dita plugins`, `dita transtypes`, `dita install`, `dita uninstall <id>`, `dita validate --input=...`, `dita version`, `dita deliverables <project>`, `dita init`, and help via `dita --help` or `dita <subcommand> --help`.

Logging and diagnostics: `--verbose` / `-v`, `--debug` / `-d`, `--logfile=file` / `-l`, optional `--logger=json`, `--stacktrace` (with verbose/debug), `--no-color` or `NO_COLOR` / `TERM=dumb`. Use `--repeat=N` to benchmark repeated runs.

Use this chunk for questions about `dita` CLI syntax, `-i`/`-f`, output directory, property files, resources, filters, temp dir, transtype list, and how AEM Guides DITA-OT presets relate to these same parameters when passed as additional command-line arguments.

Source: DITA Open Toolkit development documentation — Configuring — DITA command arguments.
list_items: Resources: `--resource` / `-r` for partial sets with extra maps or topics.
DITAVAL: `--filter=` with OS-specific multi-path rules or repeated `--filter`.

title: DITA Open Toolkit 4.4 Release Notes
content:
DITA Open Toolkit 4.4 Release Notes

The DITA-OT release notes are the first trusted source to check when a publishing pipeline changes after an upgrade. DITA-OT releases use semantic versioning: major versions may include incompatible API changes, minor versions add backward-compatible functionality, and patch versions are maintenance releases. The current development documentation identifies DITA-OT 4.4 as released January 31, 2026 and notes that DITA-OT 4.4 requires Java 17 or later. The release adds and changes DITA 2.0 preview processing, including support for the DITA 2.0 <keytext> element and recognition of the DITA 2.0 <linktitle> element. Use this page for upgrade triage, plugin compatibility checks, changed defaults, new warnings, known fixes, and questions such as why output differs after moving to DITA-OT 4.4. A senior troubleshooting answer should tell the user to compare the old and new DITA-OT versions, verify Java version, run with verbose logging, check release-note issue links for related regressions, and reproduce with a minimal map before changing content.

title: Markdown input
content:
Markdown input

DITA Open Toolkit supports Markdown files as authoring input. A Markdown topic can be referenced from a DITA map by using a normal topic reference and setting format="markdown", for example <topicref href="markdown-dita-topic.md" format="markdown"/>. During publishing to formats such as HTML or PDF, DITA-OT temporarily converts the Markdown source to DITA in the background; the original Markdown file remains the source file. DITA-OT also supports converting Markdown input to normalized DITA by running a transform with --format=dita, which is useful when a one-off Markdown contribution should be converted into DITA XML and then enriched with DITA-only semantics such as profiling attributes, conkeyref, or complex reuse. The page distinguishes the older Markdown DITA flavor from MDITA, the Markdown representation associated with Lightweight DITA drafts. Use this source for questions about Markdown topicrefs, format=markdown, Markdown-to-DITA conversion, mixed DITA and Markdown publications, and why some DITA semantics require conversion to XML.

title: Markdown DITA syntax
content:
Markdown DITA syntax

DITA-OT Markdown DITA is the original DITA-OT Markdown flavor for converting Markdown content to DITA and back. It is selected in maps with format="markdown", for example <topicref href="markdown-dita-topic.md" format="markdown"/>. Markdown DITA uses CommonMark plus DITA-specific extensions and files must be UTF-8 encoded. Heading levels generate DITA topics and titles; if an explicit ID is not supplied with header attributes, the topic ID is generated from the title. Header attributes can set id, outputclass, and profiling attributes such as audience. Level-1 heading classes such as .concept, .task, and .reference select built-in DITA specialization types. Heading classes .section and .example generate section and example elements. MultiMarkdown tables convert to the OASIS exchange table model, but table cells support only inline content and column spans; block content and row spans are not supported in Markdown DITA. Markdown DITA maps can be authored with YAML front matter using $schema: urn:oasis:names:tc:dita:xsd:map.xsd; unordered list items create topicref elements and ordered lists create topicref elements with collection-type="sequence". Link reference definitions can create key definitions, but unlike XML DITA, Markdown does not support defining keys in topic references. Links to DITA or Markdown files use DITA URI-based addressing, including fragment syntax such as filename.md#topicID/sectionID. YAML metadata can populate DITA prolog metadata such as author, source, publisher, permissions, audience, category, keyword, and resourceid; unrecognized keys are output as data elements. Use this source for senior answers about Markdown DITA syntax, Markdown topic IDs, map syntax, key definitions, key references, reltables, YAML metadata, table limitations, and Markdown-to-DITA conversion behavior.

title: Preview support for Lightweight DITA
content:
Preview support for Lightweight DITA

DITA-OT provides preview support for Lightweight DITA, or LwDITA. XDITA, MDITA, and HDITA are alternative representations of DITA content in XML, Markdown, and HTML5. The LwDITA specification has not yet been released as a formal specification, so DITA-OT support for XDITA, MDITA, and HDITA is preliminary and subject to change as LwDITA evolves. XDITA is the XML-based LwDITA authoring format; to apply XDITA-specific processing, reference the topic from a DITA map with format="xdita", for example <topicref href="xdita-topic.xml" format="xdita"/>. MDITA is the Markdown-based LwDITA format; to use stricter LwDITA-specific Markdown processing, set format="mdita", for example <topicref href="mdita-topic.md" format="mdita"/>. MDITA includes core and extended profile concepts, with parser support provided by the org.lwdita plug-in. HDITA is the HTML5-based LwDITA format; set format="hdita", for example <topicref href="hdita-topic.html" format="hdita"/>. HDITA map format is not yet supported, so include HDITA content from an XDITA map or a standard DITA map. For conditional processing in MDITA and HDITA, use data-props in source content rather than the XML @props attribute. When LwDITA topics are added to a DITA publication, DITA-OT temporarily converts them to DITA in the background for outputs such as HTML or PDF, while the source files remain unchanged. To permanently convert LwDITA and DITA XML input to normalized DITA, run a transform with --format=dita and copy the generated DITA files into the project if needed.

title: HDITA map limitations in LwDITA
content:
HDITA map limitations in LwDITA

DITA-OT preview support for Lightweight DITA includes HDITA topics, but the HDITA map format is not yet supported. To include HDITA content in a publication, use an XDITA map or a standard DITA map and reference the HTML5 topic with format="hdita", for example <topicref href="hdita-topic.html" format="hdita"/>. This is DITA-OT/LwDITA implementation guidance, not a general DITA XML map rule. In a senior troubleshooting answer, tell the user not to create an HDITA map directly; verify the root map type, the topicref @format value, and whether the HDITA source is being converted in the DITA-OT preprocessing stage.

title: DITA-OT Normalized DITA transform
content:
DITA-OT Normalized DITA transform

The DITA-OT dita transformation generates normalized DITA topics and maps from DITA input. Use it when you need to inspect effective processed content rather than authored source XML. Normalized DITA includes results of preprocessing operations such as map reference resolution, key resolution, content reference resolution, code reference resolution, and metadata movement between maps and topics. A senior troubleshooting answer should distinguish source XML from normalized/effective DITA: if the source looks correct but output fails, generate normalized DITA with --format=dita and inspect resolved keys, conrefs, filters, topicrefs, and metadata before blaming the PDF/HTML transform.

title: DITA-OT standard DITA XML input
content:
DITA-OT standard DITA XML input

DITA-OT supports released versions of the OASIS DITA specification, including DITA 1.0, 1.1, 1.2, and 1.3. In DITA-OT 4.4, the docs also describe initial preview support for draft DITA 2.0 features. For enterprise answers, keep DITA specification behavior separate from DITA-OT implementation/version behavior: DITA 1.2 and 1.3 are stable specification versions; DITA 2.0 support in current DITA-OT docs is preview behavior and should not be stated as a universal DITA rule. Use this source for questions about which DITA versions DITA-OT can process and when a failure might be caused by using draft or preview constructs.

title: DITA-OT publishing workflow
content:
DITA-OT publishing workflow

DITA-OT publishing runs source maps/topics through preprocessing and then a selected transformation type such as HTML5, PDF/PDF2, or normalized DITA. Human troubleshooting should ask for the root map, DITA-OT version, Java version, exact command, transform type, filter files, property files, plugins, and the first error in the log. Compare source XML, normalized DITA, and final output artifacts. If HTML succeeds but PDF fails, suspect transform-specific handling after preprocessing such as images, fonts, tables, generated links, FO/PDF layout, or custom PDF plugins; do not answer with a generic DITA element definition.

title: MDITA syntax in DITA-OT
content:
MDITA syntax in DITA-OT

The mdita format is the LwDITA Markdown format. To apply stricter LwDITA-specific processing to a Markdown topic, reference it from a map with format="mdita". In MDITA, the first paragraph is treated as shortdesc, tables are converted to DITA simpletable elements, and files must be UTF-8 encoded. MDITA uses CommonMark and follows the LwDITA extended profile by default; a core profile can be enabled through custom parser configuration. MDITA maps use the mditamap file extension; both ordered and unordered list items create topicref elements. For questions comparing MDITA with Markdown DITA, say MDITA is the LwDITA-constrained flavor, while markdown is the older Markdown DITA flavor with additional DITA-specific extensions.

title: Markdown DITA vs MDITA format comparison
content:
Markdown DITA vs MDITA format comparison

DITA-OT documents differences between the original Markdown DITA format and MDITA for LwDITA. Markdown DITA and MDITA share common Markdown syntax, but differ in topic structure, map syntax, tables, raw DITA support, list handling, and which extensions are available. A senior answer should not treat format="markdown" and format="mdita" as synonyms. Use format="markdown" for the older Markdown DITA behavior and format="mdita" for stricter LwDITA Markdown processing. When users ask why a Markdown table becomes table versus simpletable, or why first paragraph is body text versus shortdesc, retrieve this comparison plus the specific syntax page.

title: DITA 1.3 cascading metadata attributes in a map
content:
DITA 1.3 cascading metadata attributes in a map

In DITA 1.3, certain map-level metadata attributes cascade through the containment hierarchy of a DITA map. Cascading means values set on a map or topicref apply to child elements unless overridden by more specific effective values. Attributes that cascade include profiling metadata such as audience, platform, product, otherprops, and rev, as well as format, scope, type, processing-role, and cascade. The cascade attribute modifies additive merging behavior but does not turn cascading off completely. cascade="merge" is the processing default and values are additive; cascade="nomerge" prevents adding inherited values for an attribute when a new local value is encountered. The processing order resolves conref/keyref, explicit values, defaults, controlled values, then cascading; after attributes are resolved in a map, they cascade to referenced maps with additional map-to-map rules.

title: DITA 1.2 cascading attributes and metadata in a map
content:
DITA 1.2 cascading attributes and metadata in a map

DITA 1.2 also defines cascading of attributes and metadata in DITA maps. The DITA 1.2 architecture describes cascading for audience, platform, product, otherprops, rev, format, scope, type, processing-role, and metadata elements such as audience, category, prodinfo, and othermeta. Cascading applies to children in the containment hierarchy, not to every element type globally. The DITA 1.2 processing order evaluates conref and keyref first, then explicit values, then defaults, then cascading. Senior answers should mention version scope: DITA 1.2 has cascading behavior, but DITA 1.3 adds/clarifies the cascade attribute merge/nomerge controls, so do not apply DITA 1.3 cascade token details blindly to a DITA 1.2-only environment.

title: DITA 1.3 common map attributes
content:
DITA 1.3 common map attributes

The DITA 1.3 common map attributes page defines attributes used on many map elements and topicref specializations. Important attributes for expert chatbot answers include cascade, processing-role, linking, toc, print, search, chunk, copy-to, keyscope, and others. cascade controls how metadata attributes cascade in a map. processing-role controls whether referenced content is normal processing content or resource-only. linking controls participation in link generation, while toc controls table-of-contents/navigation inclusion; neither should be confused with output generation by itself. chunk controls how topics are combined or split during output processing. keyscope marks boundaries for scoped key definitions. Use this source when the user asks about map attributes, topicref behavior, resource-only semantics, keyscope, chunking, or why toc/linking/processing-role have different output effects.

title: DITA 1.3 other common attributes
content:
DITA 1.3 other common attributes

DITA 1.3 common attributes are used across many elements, but they are not one universal group that applies identically everywhere. Elements include only the attributes allowed by their grammar. Senior answers should avoid saying every DITA element supports every common attribute. Commonly discussed attributes include id, conref, conkeyref, keyref, outputclass, translate, xml:lang, dir, and localization/filtering-related metadata depending on the element. Always verify the specific element and DITA version before claiming an attribute is allowed. This source is useful when users ask why an attribute validates on topicref but not on entry, why conref/conkeyref behavior depends on allowed content, or why outputclass is not semantic metadata.

title: DITA 1.3 metadata in maps and topics
content:
DITA 1.3 metadata in maps and topics

DITA 1.3 metadata can be specified both in a topic and in the map that references the topic. By default, metadata in the map can supplement or override metadata specified at topic level, unless lockmeta="no" on topicmeta changes reconciliation behavior. This is central to understanding source XML versus effective metadata: a topic file may not contain an audience/product/category value, but the effective publication context can add metadata from map topicmeta or ancestor topicrefs. Senior answers should tell users to inspect the root map and effective map context, not only the standalone topic, when metadata appears in output, search, filtering, or generated navigation.

title: AEM Guides Cloud Service DITA-OT single-topic PDF generation
content:
AEM Guides Cloud Service DITA-OT single-topic PDF generation

This Experience League page explains how administrators can enable the older DITA-OT based PDF generation action from topic preview mode in AEM Guides Cloud Service. Native PDF is the default PDF generation method in current AEM Guides versions, but DITA-OT PDF can be exposed by editing the Web Editor UI configuration. The workflow is: sign in as an administrator, open Tools > Guides > Folder Profiles, open the Global Profile, edit XML Editor Configuration, download ui_config.json, replace the preview PDF button action from EDITOR_SAVE_AS_PDF to DOWNLOAD_TOPIC_PDF, save and upload the updated configuration, then choose the same folder profile in Editor user preferences. Use this source for questions about Cloud Service, Web Editor configuration, single-topic PDF preview, enabling old DITA-OT PDF generation, or why the PDF preview action uses Native PDF by default.

title: AEM Guides Editor Configuration and UI config conversion
content:
AEM Guides Editor Configuration and UI config conversion

This Experience League advanced user guide page explains how to migrate old AEM Guides ui_config customizations to the newer modular XML Editor UI configuration framework. When moving from the old UI to the new AEM Guides UI, updates in ui_config must be converted into flexible JSON files for widgets such as editor_toolbar, editor_tab_bar, file_mode_switcher, map_console_navigation_bar, map_console_action_bar, and home_navigation_bar. Each JSON uses an id for the widget, targetEditor to control when a component appears, and target to append, prepend, replace, or hide a component. The page documents targetEditor properties such as mode, displayMode, editor, documentType, documentSubType, and flag. The conversion workflow is: open Tools > Guides > Folder Profiles, select a folder profile, open XML Editor Configuration, then use Convert UI config to JSON. The conversion generates modular JSON such as editor_toolbar and map_console_action_bar. Toolbar/topbar changes go to editor_toolbar; Presets or Translation button changes go to map_console_action_bar. Use this source for questions about converting ui_config, modular JSONs, toolbar customization, targetEditor rules, DOWNLOAD_TOPIC_PDF buttons, and uploading customized JSON or CSS in AEM Guides.

title: AEM Guides UI config targetEditor properties
content:
AEM Guides UI config targetEditor properties

The targetEditor object in AEM Guides modular UI configuration controls where a customized UI component is shown after converting old ui_config customizations to JSON. Use targetEditor to scope a button, toolbar item, or action to specific editor contexts instead of showing it everywhere. Important properties include mode, displayMode, editor, documentType, documentSubType, and flag. mode is used for states such as preview or edit. displayMode controls the authoring display mode, editor scopes the component to editors such as XML editor or map editor contexts, documentType and documentSubType restrict behavior to DITA maps, topics, or specialized document types, and flag is used for feature/context flags. Senior guidance: do not put all migrated actions into one global toolbar rule. Place each action in the correct modular JSON, then use targetEditor to make the action appear only in the intended context. For example, a PDF export action that should appear only in XML preview mode should include targetEditor rules for XML/DITA map editor context and preview mode. Use this source when users ask why a toolbar button appears in the wrong place, how to scope DOWNLOAD_TOPIC_PDF, or how targetEditor differs from target append/prepend/replace behavior.

title: DITA-OT architecture and processing pipeline
content:
DITA-OT architecture and processing pipeline

DITA Open Toolkit is an open-source implementation of the OASIS DITA specification. Its architecture uses Ant, XSLT, and Java to transform DITA maps and topics into deliverable formats. DITA-OT processing is multi-stage and map-driven: stages examine source content, create or update temporary working files, and pass those temporary results to later stages. The source files themselves are not modified. DITA-OT supports map-first preprocessing as an alternative to the default preprocess operation. The processing pipeline is implemented as Ant targets, with modules implemented in Java or XSLT depending on performance and customization needs. The processing order matters; DITA-OT applies filtering before conref resolution because that order best matches user expectations, although the DITA specification does not require one universal processor order. DITA-OT extension happens through plug-ins: Ant targets can be inserted before or after common processing, and XSLT rules can override default processing. HTML-based transforms run preprocessing and then generate HTML/navigation outputs. PDF/PDF2 processing runs preprocessing, creates merged content, converts it to XSL-FO, and formats the FO to PDF. Use this source for DITA-OT architecture, preprocessing, map-first processing, plug-ins, extension points, Store API, HTML processing modules, and PDF processing modules.

title: DITA-OT processing structure
content:
DITA-OT processing structure

DITA-OT implements a multi-stage, map-driven architecture for processing DITA maps and topics. Each processing stage examines some or all content. Some stages create temporary files used by later steps, while other stages create updated copies of DITA content for downstream processing. Most processing happens in a temporary working directory; the original source files themselves are not modified. DITA-OT is designed as a pipeline. Most of the pipeline is common to all output formats and is known as the pre-processing stage. In general, any DITA process begins with this shared pre-processing set. After pre-processing completes, the pipeline diverges based on the requested output format. Some later processing is still shared by multiple formats; for example, Eclipse Help and HTML Help can share XHTML topic generation before branching to create different navigation files. Other output formats can add their own processing steps. Use this source when users ask about DITA-OT processing structure, temporary files, whether source files are modified, preprocessing, common pipeline stages, and how output-specific processing branches after common preprocessing.

title: DITA-OT map-first pre-processing
content:
DITA-OT map-first pre-processing

DITA-OT map-first pre-processing is an alternative to the default preprocess operation. It provides the same overall functionality as default preprocessing but uses a different processing approach. The default routine handles maps and topics together, often switching between map operations and topic operations. The map-first approach delays topic processing until nearly all map processing is complete. This simplifies module responsibilities and makes it easier to process only topics that remain referenced after filtering, or to validate only the map structure. Map-first processing is especially relevant because DITA 1.2 and 1.3 introduced more map-level features, including keys and key scopes, which are difficult to handle reliably before map-level features are resolved. The newer model uses hashed topic filenames in the temporary directory and better supports topics referenced outside the map directory. As of DITA-OT 3.0, map-first preprocessing is enabled by default for PDF and HTML Help; as of DITA-OT 4.2 it is enabled for HTML5 and Normalized DITA output and supports additional subject scheme features. Custom transformations can call the preprocess2 Ant target instead of preprocess. Limitation: preprocess.*.pre and preprocess.*.post extension points from the original preprocess pipeline are not available in preprocess2.
codeblocks:
<target name="dita2myhtml"
        depends="myhtml.init,
                 html5.init,
                 build-init,
                 preprocess2,
                 html5.topic,
                 html5.map,
                 html5.css"/>

title: DITA-OT processing pipeline modules
content:
DITA-OT processing pipeline modules

The DITA-OT processing pipeline is implemented using Ant. Individual modules in the Ant script are implemented in Java or XSLT depending on performance needs and customization requirements. Almost all Ant and XSLT modules can be extended by adding a plug-in to the toolkit. Plug-ins can insert new Ant targets before or after common processing, and can import new rules into common XSLT modules to override default processing. XSLT modules normally use shell files: each shell imports common rules that apply to general topics, then imports additional overrides for DITA specializations such as reference, task, highlighting domain, or local plug-in specializations. Java modules are used when XSLT is not a good fit, such as processes that depend on Java libraries, index sorting, copying files, parsing source files, or copying resources into a temporary processing directory. Use this source when users ask about DITA-OT processing modules, Ant targets, XSLT shell files, Java modules, plug-in extension of modules, specialization overrides, or how default processing is overridden.

title: DITA-OT processing order
content:
DITA-OT processing order

Processing order is significant when evaluating DITA content. The DITA specification does not mandate one universal processing order, but DITA-OT intentionally performs filtering before conref resolution because this best matches user expectations. If an element such as <note conref="documentA.dita#doc/note" product="MyProd"/> is filtered out first, DITA-OT can discard it immediately and does not need to parse the conref target document. This saves time, avoids unnecessary conref resolution, and can allow a build or translation package to succeed without unused referenced files. If conref were resolved before filtering, results could differ: attributes from the conref target might override local attributes, or a target that would later be filtered could still affect the resolved content. DITA-OT therefore treats filtering-before-conref as its chosen implementation order; another legal DITA processor could use a different order and produce different results. Senior answers should distinguish DITA specification behavior from DITA-OT implementation behavior and should not claim that all DITA processors must follow DITA-OT processing order.
codeblocks:
<note conref="documentA.dita#doc/note" product="MyProd"/>
<note id="note" product="SomeOtherProduct">This is an important note!</note>

title: DITA-OT Store API processing in memory
content:
DITA-OT Store API processing in memory

The DITA-OT Store API, org.dita.dost.store.Store, is a Java abstraction over temporary file operations. Older DITA-OT processing assumed resources were on disk and addressed by file paths. DITA-OT 3.6 introduced the Store API so temporary resources can be handled in memory rather than always being written to disk. The file-based Stream Store remains the default for backwards compatibility and uses the dita.temp.dir path; it is activated with store-type=file. The Cache Store keeps temporary resources in memory and can cache parsed XML as DOM Document or Saxon S9api XdmNode, avoiding repeated parsing when resources are read again. It can be activated with store-type=memory. In-memory processing can improve performance in I/O-bound environments such as cloud platforms, but not all custom plug-ins work with Cache Store because some assume direct file access. Custom plug-ins should use DITA-OT XSLT modules in custom pipeline elements rather than Ant built-in xslt tasks to benefit from the Store API.

title: DITA-OT pre-processing modules
content:
DITA-OT pre-processing modules

The DITA-OT pre-processing operation is a set of steps that normally runs at the beginning of every DITA-OT transformation. Each step corresponds to an Ant target in the build pipeline, and the preprocess target calls the complete set of pre-processing steps. Important modules include gen-list, debug-filter, mapref, branch-filter, keyref, copy-to, conrefpush, conref, profile, topic-fragment, chunk, move-meta-entries, mappull, maplink, topicpull, flag-module, clean-map, and copy-files. These steps prepare effective content before output-specific transforms run. For example, keyref resolves key-based links and text, conref resolves content references, profile removes content using DITAVAL or print rules, chunk assembles or splits topics based on map chunk attributes, and maplink generates map-based links from hierarchy, collection-type, and relationship tables. Use this source when users ask for the list, purpose, or sequence of DITA-OT preprocessing modules.

title: DITA-OT gen-list preprocess module
content:
DITA-OT gen-list preprocess module

The gen-list step examines DITA-OT input files and creates lists of topics, images, document properties, and other content for later pipeline stages. It is implemented in Java. For example, gen-list creates a list of topics that use @conref so only those files need to be processed during the conref stage. The generated list file name is derived from a list file property; for example, conreffile produces conref.list, and the corresponding property is conreflist. gen-list creates several list files in the temporary directory, including dita.list and dita.xml.properties. Common generated list files include conref.list for documents with conref attributes, fullditamapandtopic.list for all map and topic files referenced during transformation, fullditamap.list, fullditatopic.list, hrefditatopic.list, hreftargets.list, html.list for resource files, image.list for referenced images, resourceonly.list, subjectscheme.list, and others. Use this source when users ask which preprocess step discovers referenced files or creates conref/image/topic/resource lists.

title: DITA-OT debug-filter preprocess module
content:
DITA-OT debug-filter preprocess module

The debug-filter step processes all referenced DITA content and creates copies in the temporary directory. As the content is copied, DITA-OT performs filtering, inserts debugging information, and adjusts table column names. This step is implemented in Java and is part of the common DITA-OT preprocessing pipeline before output-specific transforms run. Use this source when users ask which preprocess module copies referenced DITA content, where filtering is applied while copying topics, which step inserts debug information, or why table column names may be adjusted in temporary DITA files. Senior answers should distinguish this DITA-OT implementation behavior from DITA specification behavior: the DITA specification defines vocabulary and semantics, while DITA-OT defines this concrete preprocessing step.

title: DITA-OT mapref preprocess module
content:
DITA-OT mapref preprocess module

The mapref step resolves map references in the DITA-OT preprocessing pipeline. In DITA-OT, elements that reference another map are replaced by the topicref elements from the referenced map. Relationship tables from the referenced map are also pulled into the referencing map. This is part of common preprocessing before output-specific transforms run, so final navigation, link generation, keys, and downstream map processing operate on an integrated effective map rather than on the originally authored map-reference boundary alone. Use this source when users ask what the mapref preprocessing step does, how submaps are integrated, whether referenced map topicrefs become part of the parent map, or why relationship tables from a submap affect the final publication. Senior answers should distinguish DITA-OT implementation behavior from the DITA specification and should not confuse the mapref preprocessing module with the DITA map-reference domain element name.

title: DITA-OT branch-filter preprocess module
content:
DITA-OT branch-filter preprocess module

The branch-filter step filters topics using DITAVAL files that are defined in the map. It is part of the DITA-OT common preprocessing pipeline and is used when map branches carry their own filtering context, such as through ditavalref-based branch filtering. Branch filtering can cause the same source topic or map branch to produce different effective content in different branches because each branch can be filtered with a different DITAVAL context. Use this source when users ask how DITA-OT applies DITAVAL rules defined in a map, why a topic appears in one branch but not another, how branch filtering differs from one global DITAVAL file, or why effective content can differ across branches. Senior answers should distinguish DITA-OT branch-filter preprocessing from the DITA specification vocabulary and should explain that downstream modules operate on branch-filtered effective content.

title: DITA-OT keyref preprocess module
content:
DITA-OT keyref preprocess module

The keyref step examines all defined keys in the effective map and resolves key references. During this DITA-OT preprocessing step, key-based link targets are resolved by replacing the key reference with the effective @href target from the key definition, and key-based text replacement is performed where appropriate. This means downstream preprocessing and output transforms work with effective resolved link targets and key-derived text rather than only the authored @keyref token. Use this source when users ask which module resolves @keyref, how key-defined @href values become link targets, why keyref requires a map context, why key text changes during processing, or why a key resolves differently after filtering, branch filtering, or key-scope changes. Senior answers should distinguish DITA key-space semantics from DITA-OT's concrete keyref preprocessing module.
